# Title slide

![](logo.jpg){width=40%}

---

## Why this study?

- Kenya’s biodiversity is legendary.
- But how much of it is actually *visible* in open data?
- Based on **4.9M GBIF records**, this reveals how sampling shapes what we think we know.

---

## Scope of Data

- Uses **ONLY GBIF-mediated open-access data** for Kenya.
- Excludes national datasets (KWS, WRTI, NMK, universities, conservancies).
- This is **“Kenya through the GBIF window”**, not a full inventory.

---

## Discovery 1 — Limited Coverage

Only **13.3%** of Kenya has any biodiversity records in GBIF.

```{r discovery1-map, fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
# reuse the same grid used in the article's leaflet map
hex_grid <- readRDS(here(results_dir, "spatial_bias", "spatial_grid_effort.rds"))

ggplot(hex_grid) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = log10(n_records + 1)), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#f0f0f0", "#e9945b", "#065f46"),
    name = "log10(records + 1)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling effort across Kenya",
    subtitle = "Hexagonal grid (~10 km). Many areas have no records."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Discovery 2 — Taxonomic Bias

**87.5% of all records are birds.**

```{r discovery2-treemap, fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
ggplot(
  class_summary,
  aes(
    area  = n_records,
    fill  = kingdom,
    label = paste(class, "\n", scales::comma(n_records), "records")
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white") +
  geom_treemap_text(colour = "white", reflow = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Taxonomic representation in Kenya's GBIF data",
    subtitle = "Aves dominates",
    fill = "Kingdom"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Discovery 3 — Data Quality Issues

```{r discovery3-quality, fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
ggplot(data_quality$tracking, aes(x = issue, y = records_flagged)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Data quality flags",
    x = "",
    y = "Records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Discovery 4 — Environmental Bias

```{r discovery4-env, fig.height=6, fig.width=8}
env_long <- env_comparison %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(elevation, temperature, precipitation),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value))

ggplot(env_long, aes(x = value, colour = type, fill = type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("available" = "#888888", "sampled" = "#065f46")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("available" = "#cccccc", "sampled" = "#a5d6c2")) +
  labs(
    title = "Environmental bias in sampling",
    subtitle = "Sampled locations represent a narrow slice of Kenya's environmental conditions."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

## Implications for Kenya

- Gaps form a **roadmap** for:
  - Strategic biodiversity surveys
  - Bias-aware modelling
  - Better conservation planning
- Helps distinguish “species absent” from “species unsampled”.

---

## Vision 2030 Alignment

- Vision 2030 calls for:
  - Mapping wildlife hotspots
  - Enhancing ecological monitoring
  - Developing a national wildlife database at KWS HQ
- This GBIF baseline complements national data systems.

---

## Global Context

Findings mirror global patterns described by:
- Meyer et al. (2015)
- Beck et al. (2014)
- Oliver et al. (2021)
- Hughes (2021)

---

## Conclusion

Kenya’s biodiversity is richer than open data suggests.
Understanding what is **missing** strengthens research, policy and conservation decisions.
